blocks.content: The story starts with two different questions that sound like one. A user arrives at your system and says: "I want to access the admin dashboard."
Your system needs to answer two completely separate questions before deciding what to do.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028048-226029668.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart showing a request branching into two separate questions: authentication (who are you) and authorization (what can you do), converging into one access decision

blocks.content:
["Question one: Who are you? Are you actually who you claim to be? This is authentication the process of verifying identity. You might check a password, a fingerprint, a cryptographic token. The answer is a yes or no: either you are who you say you are, or you're not.
","Question two: What are you allowed to do? Even if you've proven you're Alice, does Alice have permission to access the admin dashboard? This is authorisation the process of checking permissions. The answer depends on roles, policies, and what the system has been configured to allow.
"]
items: Question one: Who are you? Are you actually who you claim to be? This is authentication the process of verifying identity. You might check a password, a fingerprint, a cryptographic token. The answer is a yes or no: either you are who you say you are, or you're not.

Question two: What are you allowed to do? Even if you've proven you're Alice, does Alice have permission to access the admin dashboard? This is authorisation the process of checking permissions. The answer depends on roles, policies, and what the system has been configured to allow.

blocks.content: These are different questions. They happen at different times. They use different mechanisms. They fail in different ways.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028312-128951534.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart showing authentication happening once at login while authorization is checked repeatedly on every subsequent request

blocks.content: Confusing them leads to systems that are either too open (anyone who logs in can do anything) or too closed (authenticated users constantly hit permission walls). Getting both right and understanding how they interact is one of the most important design decisions in any system.
1. The Fundamental difference

Authentication: Are you who you say you are?
Authorisation: Are you allowed to do what you're trying to do?
Authentication happens first. Authorisation depends on authentication. You cannot authorise someone whose identity you haven't verified. But authentication alone doesn't grant access to anything
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028052-216650252.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart of a request failing authentication with 401 Unauthorized or failing authorization with 403 Forbidden before reaching access granted

blocks.content: The HTTP status codes make this concrete.

[" 401 Unauthorized is a misnomer it actually means authentication failure (unauthenticated, not unauthorised).
"," 403 Forbidden is the genuine authorisation failure the server knows who you are and has decided you're not allowed. Returning 401 when you mean 403 is a common mistake that confuses clients and leaks information about your permission model.
"]
items: 401 Unauthorized is a misnomer it actually means authentication failure (unauthenticated, not unauthorised).

403 Forbidden is the genuine authorisation failure the server knows who you are and has decided you're not allowed. Returning 401 when you mean 403 is a common mistake that confuses clients and leaks information about your permission model.

blocks.content: 2. Authentication: Proving identity
Authentication is the mechanism by which a system verifies that the entity making a request is who they claim to be. There are multiple factors:

["Something you know: password, PIN, security question
","Something you have: physical token, phone (TOTP), hardware key
","Something you are: fingerprint, face, voice
"]
items: Something you know: password, PIN, security question
Something you have: physical token, phone (TOTP), hardware key
Something you are: fingerprint, face, voice

blocks.content: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) combines two or more. The more factors, the harder it is for an attacker who has compromised one factor to succeed.
1. Password-based authentication
The user provides a username and password. The server checks the password against a stored hash.
it just establishes who is making the request.

Never store passwords in plaintext. Never store MD5 or SHA1 hashes.

Use bcrypt, Argon2, or scrypt adaptive hashing algorithms with work factors.bcrypt($password, cost=12)

→ $2b$12$eImiTXuWVxfM37uY4JANjQ==...
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: The work factor (cost parameter) makes hashing intentionally slow 100ms per hash is acceptable for login but makes brute-force attacks expensive. As hardware gets faster, you increase the cost factor to compensate.

The critical step after password verification: issuing a session or token. The password proves identity once. The session or token proves identity for subsequent requests without re-checking the password.
2. Sessions vs tokens: The two models
blocks.text: 2. Sessions vs tokens: The two models

blocks.content: 1. Session-Based Authentication (Stateful)
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028310-731358127.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart of session-based authentication: client login, server creates a session in Redis, returns a session ID cookie, and looks up the session on each request

blocks.content: Sessions are stateful the server stores session data and the client carries only a session ID.

The server must look up the session on every request. This requires a shared session store (Redis) if you run multiple servers, but allows instant revocation: delete the session record and the next request fails.
2. JWT Authentication (Stateless)
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028310-428854964.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart of JWT authentication: client login, server signs a JWT with claims, client sends the JWT in a header, server verifies the signature with no database lookup

blocks.content: JWTs are stateless the token contains all necessary information (claims) and is cryptographically signed. Any server can verify it without a database lookup. This enables horizontal scaling without shared state. The cost: revocation is hard.
If a user's role changes or they're banned, existing JWTs remain valid until expiry. Short expiry times (15 minutes) with refresh tokens is the standard mitigation.

blocks.content: The signature is what makes JWTs trustworthy. A server signs the token with its private key (RS256) or a shared secret (HS256). Any server with the public key can verify the signature without contacting the auth server. If someone tampers with the payload, the signature verification fails.

Never put sensitive data in a JWT payload. The payload is base64-encoded, not encrypted. Anyone who has the token can read the claims. Put only what downstream services need: user ID, roles, permissions scope. Never put passwords, PII beyond user ID, or anything that shouldn't be visible if the token is leaked.

blocks.content: 3. OAuth 2.0: Delegated authentication
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028050-603676639.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart of OAuth 2.0 actors: resource owner, third-party client app, authorization server, and resource server, showing delegated access without sharing the password

blocks.content: When a third party needs to access your resources on behalf of you, passwords don't work you don't give your Gmail password to every app that wants to read your email. OAuth 2.0 solves this.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277430037-417521051.png
blocks.alt: Sequence diagram of the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow between user, app, authorization server, and resource server, from login redirect to exchanging the code for an access token

blocks.content: OAuth 2.0 is an authorisation framework (confusingly named it handles delegated access, not identity).

OpenID Connect (OIDC) is the identity layer built on top: it adds an id_token (a JWT with user identity claims) to the OAuth flow. Together, OAuth 2.0 + OIDC is how "Login with Google/GitHub/Apple" works.
The 4 OAuth grant types serve different use cases:

["Authorization Code: web apps with a backend (the flow above)","Authorization Code + PKCE: single-page apps and mobile apps (no client secret)","Client Credentials: machine-to-machine, no user involved","Device Code: TV apps, CLI tools that can't open a browser"]
items: Authorization Code: web apps with a backend (the flow above)
Authorization Code + PKCE: single-page apps and mobile apps (no client secret)
Client Credentials: machine-to-machine, no user involved
Device Code: TV apps, CLI tools that can't open a browser

blocks.content: 3. Authorisation: determining what's allowed
Once identity is established, authorisation decides what that identity can do. Three dominant models exist, each with different trade-offs.
Model 1: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)  Used by: most SaaS
blocks.text: Model 1: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)  Used by: most SaaS

blocks.content: Users are assigned to roles. Roles have permissions. You check whether the user's role has the required permission.

Users:

  Alice → roles: [admin, editor]
  Bob   → roles: [viewer]

Roles → Permissions:

  admin:  [read, write, delete, manage_users]
  editor: [read, write]
  viewer: [read]

Check: can Alice delete a post?
  Alice has admin role → admin has delete permission → YES

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277431815-814257922.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart of role-based access control: Alice with admin and editor roles gets read, write, and delete permissions, Bob with viewer role gets read-only permission

blocks.content: RBAC is the right default for most applications. Simple, auditable, fast. It breaks down when you need fine-grained control that depends on the specific resource being accessed ("Alice can edit posts she authored but not posts Bob authored") or on context ("only during business hours").

The role explosion problem: as the product grows, you create increasingly specific roles to handle edge cases. "admin," "editor," "viewer" becomes "content-admin," "regional-editor-europe," "read-only-finance-viewer," "api-user-external-partner-tier2." Maintaining these and understanding what each one can do becomes a management problem.
Model 2: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277433592-532086515.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart of attribute-based access control: subject, object, action, and environment attributes feeding into a policy engine that evaluates allow or deny

blocks.content: ABAC evaluates policies against attributes of the subject (user), object (resource), action, and environment (context). More flexible, more powerful, more complex.

Policy: "A user can edit a post if:

  - user.department = post.department
  - AND user.clearance >= post.sensitivity_level
  - AND current_time is within user.working_hours
  - AND user.status = 'active'"

Check: can Alice edit post #42?

  Alice.department = 'engineering'
  post#42.department = 'engineering'       ✓
  Alice.clearance = 3, post#42.sensitivity = 2  ✓
  current_time = 14:30, Alice.hours = 9-18  ✓
  Alice.status = 'active'                  ✓
  → ALLOW

blocks.content: ABAC can express policies that RBAC cannot context-aware, resource-owner-aware, time-aware, environment-aware.
The cost is complexity: policies are harder to write, harder to audit, and slower to evaluate than role lookups. Mistakes in policy expression can create security holes that are non-obvious.

AWS IAM is the canonical example of ABAC at scale. IAM policies evaluate conditions (StringEquals, IpAddress, DateLessThan) against resource ARNs, request contexts, and user attributes. It's powerful enough to express almost any permission model, and complex enough to be a career specialisation.
Model 3: Policy-based access control with an external engine
blocks.text: Model 3: Policy-based access control with an external engine

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028047-416700139.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart of a policy-based access control architecture where application code asks an external policy engine like OPA for an allow or deny decision and enforces it

blocks.content: The modern evolution: extract all authorisation logic into a dedicated policy engine.
Application code asks "can user X do action Y on resource Z?" The policy engine evaluates and returns allow/deny. Application code enforces the decision.

["Open Policy Agent (OPA) is the leading open-source policy engine. You write policies in Rego (a declarative language). The application calls OPA via HTTP or gRPC. OPA evaluates against data and returns a decision.
","Casbin is a popular library that implements RBAC, ABAC, and other models with a model definition file.
","AWS Cedar: Amazon's policy language for their Verified Permissions service.
"]
items: Open Policy Agent (OPA) is the leading open-source policy engine. You write policies in Rego (a declarative language). The application calls OPA via HTTP or gRPC. OPA evaluates against data and returns a decision.
Casbin is a popular library that implements RBAC, ABAC, and other models with a model definition file.
AWS Cedar: Amazon's policy language for their Verified Permissions service.

blocks.content: The advantage: policy logic is centralised, auditable, testable, and versionable separately from application code. You can change who can do what without deploying application code. The disadvantage: network round-trip per authorisation decision (mitigated by caching or embedding the engine as a library).
4. Resource ownership: the common case RBAC misses
blocks.text: 4. Resource ownership: the common case RBAC misses

blocks.content: One of the most frequent real-world authorisation requirements: a user can modify their own resources but not others'. "Alice can edit her own posts. Bob can edit his own posts. Neither can edit the other's."
This is trivially wrong with pure role-based checks:
1. Wrong: Every editor can edit every post
This approach checks only the user's role. Once someone has the EDITOR role, they can edit every post in the system, including posts created by other users.
2. Right: Editor can edit only their own posts
This approach adds an ownership check. A user must be an EDITOR and must also be the author of the post to edit it.
3. With Admin Override

This is a common real-world authorization rule. Administrators can edit any post, while editors can edit only the posts they created. This combines role-based access control with resource-level permissions.

This resource-ownership check is a form of ABAC (the resource's author_id attribute is compared to the subject's idattribute), but it's so common that most applications implement it ad-hoc rather than through a formal ABAC engine.
The danger: this logic is scattered across every endpoint that needs ownership checks, making it easy to miss one and create a privilege escalation vulnerability.
The pattern to use: centralise ownership checks in a reusable function or service layer, and test it explicitly.
5. Where authentication and authorisation live in the architecture
blocks.text: 5. Where authentication and authorisation live in the architecture

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277437022-579877756.png
blocks.alt: Flowchart showing authentication handled once at the API gateway which validates the JWT and injects trusted headers, while downstream services perform fine-grained authorization checks

blocks.content: The pattern used at scale:

["Authentication once at the gateway. The API gateway validates the JWT, extracts claims (user ID, roles, scopes), and injects them as trusted headers (X-User-Id, X-User-Roles) for downstream services. Services never see the raw token they trust the gateway's extracted claims.
","Coarse-grained authorisation at the gateway. Role-level checks that apply uniformly to endpoints: \"only admin role can access /admin/\", \"only authenticated users can access /api/\". These don't require knowledge of specific resources.
","Fine-grained authorisation in the service. Resource-level checks that require business logic: \"can this user edit this specific post?\" happens in the service because only the service knows the post's author and the business rules around editing.
"]
items: Authentication once at the gateway. The API gateway validates the JWT, extracts claims (user ID, roles, scopes), and injects them as trusted headers (X-User-Id, X-User-Roles) for downstream services. Services never see the raw token they trust the gateway's extracted claims.

Coarse-grained authorisation at the gateway. Role-level checks that apply uniformly to endpoints: "only admin role can access /admin/", "only authenticated users can access /api/". These don't require knowledge of specific resources.

Fine-grained authorisation in the service. Resource-level checks that require business logic: "can this user edit this specific post?" happens in the service because only the service knows the post's author and the business rules around editing.

blocks.content: This separation keeps the gateway thin and fast while allowing services to make nuanced decisions.
6. Token refresh and session management
Short-lived access tokens (15 minutes) solve the JWT revocation problem but create user experience problems users get logged out every 15 minutes. Refresh tokens solve this.

Access token:  expires in 15 minutes — used for API calls
Refresh token: expires in 30 days — used only to get new access tokens

Flow:

1. Login → receive {access_token, refresh_token}
2. Make API calls with access_token
3. access_token expires
4. Client sends refresh_token to /auth/refresh
5. Server validates refresh_token, issues new access_token
6. Client continues making API calls

Revocation:

- Revoke the refresh_token → user must re-login
- Revoke the access_token → must wait for expiry (or use denylist)

blocks.content: Refresh tokens should be stored securely (httpOnly cookies, not localStorage) and rotated on each use when you exchange a refresh token for a new access token, the old refresh token is invalidated and a new one is issued.
If the same refresh token is used twice, both tokens are revoked (indicating theft).
7. Common vulnerabilities
Broken object-level authorisation (BOLA/IDOR). The most common API security vulnerability. The endpoint checks that the user is authenticated but not that they own the resource:
Vulnerable: Any authenticated user can read any order
This endpoint only checks whether the user is authenticated. There is no ownership validation, so any logged-in user can access any order simply by changing the orderId in the URL.
Fixed: Check ownership before returning the order
This approach first loads the order and then checks whether the current user owns the order or has theADMINrole. If neither condition is true, the request is rejected with403 Forbidden.
This is a classic example of resource-level authorization, where access depends not only on the user's role but also on the specific resource being accessed.
BOLA/IDOR is #1 on the OWASP API Security Top 10. An attacker simply increments the resource ID in the URL to access other users' data.

JWT algorithm confusion. A JWT signed with RS256 (asymmetric) specifies the algorithm in the header. If the server blindly trusts the alg header and the attacker changes it to none or HS256, they can forge tokens. Fix: never trust the algorithm in the token header. Pin the algorithm in your verification code.

Privilege escalation through JWT claims. If the server trusts roles: ["admin"] in the JWT without verifying it was legitimately issued, any attacker who can craft a JWT can give themselves admin. Fix: sign JWTs with a secret only your auth server knows, and verify the signature before trusting any claims.

Overly broad tokens. An OAuth token with scope: * that grants access to everything is a security liability. If leaked, an attacker has full access. Use minimal scopes. A token for reading a user's profile should not also have permission to delete their account.
8. The Comparison

blocks.content: 9. HLD interview ( How to talk )
When designing any system with users and data, authentication and authorisation both require explicit design decisions.

Draw the distinction immediately. "Authentication and authorisation are two separate concerns. Authentication verifying identity happens at the gateway. Authorisation checking what that identity can do happens at two layers: coarse-grained role checks at the gateway, fine-grained resource-level checks in each service."

On token choice: "I'd use JWTs for service-to-service calls and for stateless API authentication. Short-lived access tokens (15 minutes) with rotating refresh tokens (30 days) handle the revocation tradeoff most role changes take effect within 15 minutes without needing a token denylist."

On the authorisation model: "For a multi-tenant SaaS product, I'd start with RBAC roles like admin, member, viewer within each organisation. Roles cover 80% of cases and are simple to audit. For the edge cases that RBAC can't express — like 'a user can only edit documents they created' I'd add resource ownership checks in the service layer as a standard pattern, not scattered ad-hoc."

On the architecture: "The gateway handles authentication it validates the JWT, extracts user_id and roles, and injects them as headers. Downstream services trust these headers and focus on business logic. They never re-verify the JWT themselves. For fine-grained checks 'can this user access this specific order?' the order service checks ownership against its own data."

On security: "The most common mistake I'd guard against is BOLA checking that a user is authenticated but not that they own the resource they're requesting. Every endpoint that returns or modifies a resource needs an explicit ownership check. I'd enforce this with code review checklists and integration tests that specifically verify that user A cannot access user B's resources."

The deepest insight: "Authentication tells you who. Authorisation tells you what. They're separate concerns with separate failure modes, separate testing requirements, and separate maintenance surfaces. Conflating them leads to systems that are either too permissive (authentication implying full access) or impossible to audit (authorisation logic spread everywhere with no clear model)."
